entities.summary:
Pope Leo X was the head of the Catholic Church and ruler of the Papal States from 9 March 1513 to his death in December 1521. He was born around 1475 and became pope at the age of 38, following the death of his predecessor, Pope Julius II. Leo X's papacy was marked by a series of conflicts with the Holy Roman Emperor, Charles V, and the Ottoman Empire, which threatened the stability of the Italian peninsula. The papacy also saw significant cultural and artistic developments, including the works of the Italian Renaissance artist Raphael, who was appointed as the papal painter.

Leo X's reign was also marked by the Sack of Rome in 1527, which was carried out by troops loyal to Charles V. The sack resulted in significant damage to the city and the loss of many lives. Despite this, Leo X continued to exercise significant influence over the Catholic Church and the Papal States until his death in December 1521.

Leo X's legacy is complex and multifaceted. On the one hand, he played a significant role in shaping the course of European history, particularly in the areas of religion and politics. On the other hand, his papacy was marked by a series of conflicts and power struggles that ultimately led to his downfall. Today, Leo X is remembered as a key figure in the history of the Catholic Church and the Papal States, and his legacy continues to be felt in the modern world.

Leo X was a member of the Medici family, which had risen to prominence in Florence during the Renaissance. He was a close friend and patron of the artist and poet, Lorenzo de' Medici, and played a significant role in promoting the arts and culture during his papacy.

The papacy of Leo X was also marked by significant theological debates, particularly over the issue of indulgences. The controversy surrounding indulgences led to a major split in the Catholic Church, with Martin Luther and John Calvin emerging as key figures in the Protestant Reformation.
